case_study_insert.main_stem: Stonebrook Fine Foods (SFF) is a partnership in the specialty preserves and condiments sector, employing a workforce of 38. Founded in 2015 by chef Daniel Stonebrook, it supplies artisan jams and chutneys to independent delicatessens and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. SFF plans to invest $640,000 in a new automated preserves bottling and labelling line, financed by a $340,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $200,000 a year, a variable cost of $3.00 a unit and a selling price of $8.00, and currently produces 90,000 units a year. SFF faces two problems: labour turnover has risen to 11% and defect rates on the labelling line are high.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report — Q4 2025: The labelling line filled 19,000 jars last quarter with a defect rate of 2.8%, up from 1.9% a year ago. Customer complaints rose from 22 to 37 per month. Average delivery time to delicatessens is 3.9 days. Ingredient waste measured 4.6% of output. Labour turnover reached 11% over the year. A survey of 500 delicatessen customers found 63% would pay up to $0.45 more for artisan preserves and 57% value distinctive labelling. Training records show 12 of 38 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new labeller; off-the-job training at the food technology centre costs $750 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Stonebrook Fine Foods as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 3.75% to 4.50%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $13.10 to $13.94 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Sugar, fruit and glass-jar input costs have risen 8.7% year-on-year, and food-price inflation is 5.8%, while consumer spending on artisan preserves grew 3.2% in the same period.

questions.question_text: SFF plans to finance part of its labelling line expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for SFF of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit costs SFF nothing in interest or capital repayments, unlike the $340,000 bank loan, which protects cash flow while the partnership already meets fixed costs of $200,000 a year. The $300,000 of retained profit can go straight into the $640,000 labelling line and helps absorb the 8.7% rise in sugar, fruit and glass-jar costs without forcing a rise in the $8.00 selling price for independent delicatessens.

Point 2: Using retained profit avoids the collateral and repossession risk of a bank loan, so the new bottling line cannot be seized if demand for artisan jams and chutneys disappoints. It also preserves Daniel Stonebrook's control of the partnership, since no lender can impose conditions on how the business operates. Because retained profit is already inside the firm, there are no arrangement fees or variable-rate exposure when the base rate rose from 3.75% to 4.50%. Overall, internal finance is cheaper and less risky than increasing the firm's borrowings.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to SFF and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: SFF is launching its new artisan preserves range. Consider a national magazine advertising campaign, local food fairs, or social media influencer marketing. Which should SFF choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National magazine advertising campaign: A magazine campaign can reach a broad, upmarket readership and build brand awareness for artisan preserves. However, national advertising is expensive for a 38-employee partnership already funding a $640,000 line with a $340,000 loan, and much of the readership will not visit independent delicatessens, so a large part of the spend would not convert into sales.

Local food fairs: Food fairs put SFF's jams and chutneys directly in front of delicatessen customers and food lovers, allow tastings, and match the 57% who value distinctive labelling and the 63% of 500 surveyed customers who would pay $0.45 more. They are relatively cheap and give immediate feedback, but reach is limited to one region at a time and cannot quickly build national awareness.

Social media influencer marketing: Food influencers can showcase artisan preserves to a targeted audience at low cost per reached buyer and can explain the premium that 63% of customers accept. Results take time and depend on credibility, and the audience may not be the delicatessen shoppers who actually buy the product.

Recommendation: SFF should choose local food fairs as the primary channel, with modest social media support. Fairs reach the exact customers who buy from delicatessens, fit a partnership with $200,000 fixed costs, and let the distinctive labelling and taste sell themselves. National magazine advertising is rejected as costly and untargeted for a small firm with loan commitments, while influencer marketing is rejected as the lead channel because its audience is diffuse and slower to convert than face-to-face tastings at fairs.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of SFF with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of SFF with a well-justified recommendation explaining why magazine advertising and influencer marketing are rejected.

questions.question_text: SFF's labour turnover has risen to 11% and defect rates are high. Explain two benefits for SFF of using democratic leadership to motivate its labelling team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the 38 employees a say in how the new labelling line is run, which satisfies social and esteem needs and raises job satisfaction. Workers who help set labelling routines are more likely to stay, directly tackling SFF's 11% labour turnover and reducing the disruption caused by constantly recruiting and training replacements.

Point 2: Consulting the operators who handle jars every day produces practical ideas to cut the 2.8% defect rate and the 4.6% ingredient waste reported in the quality report. Higher involvement raises commitment to quality, protecting the $5.00 contribution per unit and the $640,000 investment. It also lowers the need for the $750 per employee off-the-job training that follows high turnover, because experienced staff stay to coach new colleagues within SFF's hierarchical structure.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to SFF's turnover, defects and output.

questions.question_text: SFF must upskill 12 staff to operate the new labeller. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the food technology centre. Which should SFF choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training 12 staff on SFF's own labeller is directly relevant to the firm's exact settings and quality standards, costs nothing in external fees, and keeps those workers productive while they learn, protecting output toward 90,000 units and the effort to cut the 2.8% defect rate. The drawback is that trainers are themselves production staff whose work suffers, and bad habits can be passed on, which matters while complaints have risen from 22 to 37.

Off-the-job training: The food technology centre course at $750 per employee gives structured, up-to-date skills and a recognised certificate for all 12 staff, costing $9,000 in total — modest beside the $640,000 line. It removes 12 workers from the line, cutting short-term capacity and risking more labelling defects, and the generic content may not match SFF's exact machine, so follow-up coaching would still be needed.

Decision: SFF should choose on-the-job training for the initial rollout, adding short centre modules later for senior operators. On-the-job training is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids losing capacity while defect rates are high and labour turnover is 11%; full off-the-job training is rejected because withdrawing $9,000 and 12 staff from a new line would jeopardise supply to delicatessens, and SFF can add certification once the line is stable.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to SFF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of SFF.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of SFF with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how SFF's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $200,000 ÷ ($8.00 − $3.00) = $200,000 ÷ $5.00 = 40,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 40,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $8.00 − $3.00 = $5.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $5.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways SFF's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. SFF's managers can compare the 40,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 90,000 units to confirm the preserves line is profitable, giving a margin of safety of 50,000 units, which supports running the new $640,000 line near capacity.
2. Contribution per unit of $5.00 lets SFF model the $0.45 premium for artisan preserves: if won, contribution rises toward $5.45, showing how much extra volume is needed to cover $200,000 fixed costs.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $200,000 and contribution of $5.00 lets managers set the sales volume needed to service the $340,000 bank loan and check the line can afford repayments before committing more retained profit.
4. Managers can use unit cost ($200,000 ÷ 90,000 units + $3.00 = $5.22 a unit) to benchmark each quarter, isolate the 4.6% ingredient waste, and judge whether to renegotiate the $3.00 variable cost given 8.7% input-cost inflation.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 40,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $5.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 90,000-unit output; the $0.45 premium against $200,000 fixed costs; loan-repayment feasibility for the $340,000 loan; and unit-cost benchmarking at $5.22 to tackle 4.6% waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate SFF's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has SFF's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.50 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.62 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.83 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.15 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $80,000 inventories + $70,000 trade receivables + $30,000 cash = $180,000; 2025 current assets = $60,000 + $100,000 + $50,000 = $210,000. Liquidity cover for 2024 = $180,000 ÷ $120,000 = 1.50, and for 2025 = $210,000 ÷ $130,000 = 1.62. Excluding stock, 2024 = ($180,000 − $80,000) ÷ $120,000 = $100,000 ÷ $120,000 = 0.83, and 2025 = ($210,000 − $60,000) ÷ $130,000 = $150,000 ÷ $130,000 = 1.15.

Evaluation: SFF's short-term liquidity has strengthened. The first ratio rose from 1.50 to 1.62 as current assets grew from $180,000 to $210,000 while current liabilities rose only from $120,000 to $130,000, so the partnership covers its short-term debts more comfortably. The second ratio, which strips out inventories, improved from 0.83 to 1.15, so SFF is no longer reliant on selling preserve stock to meet obligations — important while it services a $340,000 bank loan and funds a $640,000 line. However, trade receivables rose from $70,000 to $100,000, tying up cash; if delicatessens pay late the improvement could reverse, and the fall in inventories to $60,000 should be watched to avoid shortages.

Conclusion: SFF's financial position has improved. Both liquidity measures moved favourably (1.50 to 1.62 and 0.83 to 1.15), and the improvement does not depend on stock. The residual risk is higher receivables, so SFF should tighten credit control with its delicatessen customers while proceeding with the labelling investment.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether SFF's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for SFF of using distinctive labelling on its artisan preserves.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Distinctive labelling appeals to the 57% of surveyed delicatessen customers who value it and supports the premium that 63% of 500 customers would pay $0.45 more for, protecting the $5.00 contribution per unit even as sugar, fruit and glass-jar costs rise 8.7%. It also differentiates SFF's jams and chutneys on delicatessen shelves, helping win repeat orders that justify the $640,000 labelling line.

Disadvantage: Distinctive labels cost more to design and print, which can lift the $3.00 variable cost per unit and squeeze margins unless the $0.45 premium is accepted. A complex label can also slow the new line and worsen the 2.8% defect rate or the 4.6% ingredient waste if jars are mislabelled, especially while labour turnover is 11% and staff are still learning the new labeller.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to SFF's research data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.50%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 8.7% rise in input costs will affect SFF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.50%): If SFF's $340,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75 percentage points × $340,000 = $2,550 a year (0.0075 × $340,000). That is small against $200,000 fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed-rate the effect is zero. Higher rates may also make consumers cautious and raise the cost of future borrowing for the $640,000 line, but SFF can limit this by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, to $13.94 an hour): SFF employs a workforce of 38 in bottling and labelling, so this rise feeds into the wage bill and cannot be avoided. No hours worked or individual pay figures are given, so a defensible annual total cannot be invented; the honest test is productivity: 90,000 units ÷ 38 staff = 2,368.42 units per worker, so the rise is affordable only if productivity holds or output grows, otherwise unit labour cost climbs and the $5.00 contribution per unit shrinks.

Input cost inflation (8.7% sugar, fruit and glass jars): SFF's $3.00 variable cost per unit contains these inputs, but the insert never decomposes it, so only a bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 8.7% that adds about 8.7% × $3.00 = $0.26 per unit, and at 90,000 units that is roughly $23,500 a year. Even a smaller rise erodes contribution, but the $0.45 premium and delicatessen price talks can recover part of it.

Conclusion: The 8.7% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact because it compounds on every one of the 90,000 jars and directly erodes the $5.00 contribution that justifies the $640,000 line, and unlike the loan it cannot be neutralised by fixing a rate. The wage rise is real but manageable if productivity holds, and the interest rise adds only about $2,550, so both are smaller.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to SFF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on SFF's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of SFF with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
